question: Every year, 100 000 children go missing in the European Union. Cross-border cooperation, both between Member States and with third countries, must therefore be improved. A European centre for missing persons could be established to make sure that this cooperation is as effective as possible.

To expedite this process, the current regulatory framework of existing agencies could be used to set up a specialised department, given that creating a new agency, establishing its regulatory framework and negotiating a location for its headquarters would waste valuable time.
My question is therefore also a proposal: could existing agencies, such as Europol or Eurojust, set up a specialised department to deal with child disappearances?
answer: The prevention and response to child disappearance is a priority for the Commission. The ‘116 000’ European hotline for missing children is available in all EU Member States and the Commission has been supporting the Missing Children Europe (1) federation through funding (2). The 2020 European Migration Network study (3) helped to identify practices and challenges in this area.

The EU Strategy on the rights of the child (4) called on the EU Member States to improve the functioning of the missing child helpline. The recommendation on integrated child protection systems (5) underlined the role of those helplines and the need to improve data collection. Eurojust supports coordination and cooperation between national investigating and prosecuting authorities on serious, crossborder crime.

It facilitates cooperation between these authorities on those cases of child disappearance that are a criminal offence falling under the forms of serious, cross-border crime listed in Annex I of the Eurojust Regulation (6) or connected offences. Eurojust has specialised teams (e.g. on human trafficking) and focus groups with representatives of Member States’ nationals authorities, (e.g. on migrant smuggling).

Since 2023, the Schengen Information System (SIS) alert mechanism can also include alerts to find missing persons, including children. Europol’s role in this area is limited by its legal framework (7).

Europol can assist Member States in finding children suspected of being illegally deported in the context of armed conflicts and support Member States’ investigations into individuals and criminal networks linked to forms of crimes for which Europol is competent. The Europol’s Executive Director can propose and the Management Board decide on new specialised departments at Europol.
